title: A Way of Thinking About Self Evaluation
author: Nick Nickhart
summary: Nick Nickhart lays out a five-part mental model for how school leaders should approach self-evaluation: gathering Facts (accountability data, curriculum results, pastoral, regulatory, finance and HR indicators), 'Mapping' those facts through physical, conceptual and temporal lenses to understand where and when phenomena occur, forming and continually revising Assumptions (deliberately asking 'how is it?' rather than the more judgement-laden 'how good is it?'), converting insight into shared Priorities anchored in common language and organisational systems, and tracking short-cycle Indicators (learning time, attention, interactions, climate) so problems surface before they compound. He closes with a caution about the Limitations of any single evaluation format, arguing that standard SEF/SIP proformas can hinder as much as help thinking and that schools may be better served designing their own fit-for-purpose recording process. The piece is explicitly framed as one leader's mental model rather than a prescriptive method, meant to be borrowed from, adapted, or rejected in parts by other school leaders.
points: Frames self-evaluation as a continuous five-stage cycle (Facts, Maps, Assumptions, Priorities, Indicators) rather than a single annual audit, explicitly rejecting the idea of one unifying evaluative model.
Recommends reframing evaluative questions from 'How good is it?' to 'How is it?' to reduce premature value judgements before enough mapping has been done to justify them.
Cites Viviane Robinson's argument that leaders should target change at the level of beliefs, not just actions, when trying to secure smooth adoption of new practices.
Identifies four concrete short-cycle indicators — learning time, attention, interactions, and climate — as early-warning signals leaders can watch for between full evaluation cycles.
Warns that standardised SEF/SIP proformas can constrain rather than sharpen leadership thinking, suggesting schools instead design their own evaluation format fit for their specific community.
quotes: The continuous cycle of understanding the reality of school life and making decisions to improve aspects of it is at the heart of school leadership.
There is no definitive map, only different ways of viewing a complex reality.
It is perhaps more appropriate to ask 'How is it?' rather than 'How good is it?' This process is very much ongoing; we'll continually be adapting our assumptions in light of refined mapping.
Aligned beliefs are necessary for smooth adoption of new or improved practices. Viviane Robinson advocates targeting change at the level of beliefs rather than actions if we are to be most effective.
Small things left unattended can become bigger problems down the line so it is prudent to have some early warning signals that things aren't working as we'd like.
Climate is a useful indicator: how do colleagues feel about their work? Are there any signs of stress, frustration or burnout?
I have for some time thought that the process of evaluation and improvement planning has been led by the proforma.
